AI-Assisted Python, DuckPad | Issue 112

A weekly curated update on data science and engineering topics and resources.





Rami Krispin
Oct 31, 2026

This week’s agenda:

  • Open Source of the Week - DuckPad

  • New learning resources - Kimi K3.1 Pro, agent harnesses, OpenCode 2.0, local AI agents on Ubuntu, and prefill-only decision models

  • Book of the week - AI-Assisted Python for Nonprogrammers by Reuven M. Lerner


The newsletter is available on LinkedIn and Substack.


Open Source of the Week

This week’s focus is on the DuckPad project.

DuckPad is an open-source SQL workspace powered by DuckDB 2.0. It turns data sources, joins, reusable components, and SQL transformations into visual pipelines you can explore and version. Rather than treating a result as the end of the workflow, DuckPad lets users select a cell and trace the source values that contributed to it. You can store projects in Git, develop on independent branches, compare them visually, and review changes before merging. The project runs on your own infrastructure and supports environment-specific connections and team access controls.

Project repo: https://github.com/hugues31/duckpad

Key Features

  • Visual pipelines — connect data sources, joins, and reusable components in a graphical workspace.

  • Integrated SQL editor — use guided forms or write SQL directly when defining transformations.

  • Cell-level lineage — trace a result cell back to the source values that contributed to it.

  • Git versioning — save projects, work on separate branches, and compare pipeline changes visually.

  • Merge review — inspect proposed changes before applying them to a project.

  • Self-hosted operation — run DuckPad on your own infrastructure and configure connections by environment.

  • Project access — manage access for teams working in the same DuckPad deployment.


More details are available in the project documentation.

License: MIT




New Learning Resources

Here are some new learning resources that I came across this week.

The Best Open Model Right Now? (Kimi K3.1 Pro)

This video from NeuralNine examines Kimi K3.1 Pro through published benchmarks and three coding tasks: a CNN training visualizer, thumbnail asset generation, and a MOBA game prototype.



What Is an Agent Harness? How AI Coding Agents Work

The following visual explainer from AI Systems with Andy breaks an agent harness into its loop, tools, context, memory, and controls. It also covers the execution cycle, context management, permissions, agents versus workflows, and a minimal Python implementation.



Harness² Explained: Self-Improving Agents Without Training

This video from Prompt Engineering examines Harness², a research framework that enables an agent to modify its prompts, skills, scripts, subagents, and control-loop hooks for each task without retraining the model. It explains the Propose, Probe, and Compose process, its experience library, comparisons with coding agents, and the approach’s limitations.



OpenCode 2.0: Biggest Update Ever (Free + Local Models)

This video from Leon van Zyl tests OpenCode 2.0 by building a bill splitter application. It covers free models, sessions shared across the terminal and desktop app, background agents, MCP code mode, Git worktrees, custom plugins, and running local models with Ollama.



Jev Course – Prefill-Only Inference & Decision Models from Scratch

This course from freeCodeCamp builds Jev-style decision models with PyTorch and Hugging Face. It covers encoder- and decoder-based architectures, custom causal attention masks, KV-cache reuse, teacher-student distillation, and reinforcement learning for structured choices, scores, and Boolean outputs.



Building a Local AI Agent in Workshop on Ubuntu

The following tutorial from Canonical Ubuntu builds a local coding agent with Canonical Workshop and the Qwen3-Coder inference snap. It demonstrates an isolated development environment, a tunnel to the locally hosted model, and coding tasks that run without an internet connection.



Agent Harness for Learning Things

This video by Eero Alvar presents LearnHarness, an agent-based system for personalized learning. It demonstrates how the system probes existing knowledge, plans a dependency path, teaches and practices in small steps, and stores propositions and reasoning chains in a persistent knowledge graph.




Book of the Week

This week’s focus is on a new book — AI-Assisted Python for Nonprogrammers by Reuven M. Lerner. The book introduces Python to readers without previous programming experience while using AI chatbots as learning partners. It builds from the concepts behind computers and programming through core Python syntax, data structures, functions, modules, and packages. Focused exercises use approaches such as strategy sessions, debugging prompts, interviews, and reverse Socratic questioning to reinforce the material. The final chapters connect these foundations to AI-assisted and agentic coding tools while emphasizing the programming knowledge needed to evaluate and maintain generated code.

Topics Covered

  • Python foundations — programming concepts, installation, IDEs, and JupyterLite.

  • Values and variables — data types, assignment, input, and formatted strings.

  • Control flow — conditions, comparisons, Boolean logic, and loops.

  • Core data structures — strings, lists, tuples, and dictionaries.

  • Files — reading, writing, parsing, and converting text into data.

  • Functions — parameters, return values, documentation, scope, and arguments.

  • Modules and namespaces — imports, aliases, and Python’s standard library.

  • Package management — evaluating PyPI packages and managing projects with uv.

  • AI-assisted coding — pair programming with chatbots and GitHub Copilot.

  • Agentic coding — working with Claude Code and OpenCode while considering code quality and maintenance.


This book is ideal for beginners and nonprogrammers who want to learn Python fundamentals while developing practical habits for working with AI coding tools.

The book is available on O’Reilly and Amazon.


Have any questions? Please comment below!

See you next Saturday!

Thanks,

Rami

issues.title: Data Engineering for Multimodal AI, Pixeltable…
issues.html:
Data Engineering for Multimodal AI, Pixeltable | Issue 111

A weekly curated update on data science and engineering topics and resources.





Rami Krispin
Oct 24, 2026

This week’s agenda:

  • Open Source of the Week - Pixeltable

  • New learning resources - Qwen RL experiments, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, terminal development setup

  • Book of the week - Data Engineering for Multimodal AI by Vasundra Srinivasan

The newsletter is available on LinkedIn and Substack.



Open Source of the Week

Pixeltable is an open-source Python project for building AI applications with images, video, audio, documents, and structured data. It combines a multimodal database, data processing, vector search, and API serving. Transformations and model calls are defined as computed columns, with their results stored alongside the source data. Pixeltable tracks column dependencies and processes new rows as they arrive. The goal is to reduce the code needed to keep media, metadata, model outputs, and search indexes in sync.

Project repo: https://github.com/pixeltable/pixeltable

Key Features

  • Multimodal tables — work with images, video, audio, and documents alongside ordinary columns.

  • Computed columns — define transformations and model calls as part of a table.

  • Incremental processing — process new data and recompute affected results without repeating unrelated work.

  • Vector search — declare embedding indexes that the table maintains as data changes.

  • Media processing — build workflows for document chunks, video frames, and audio transcripts.

  • Versioning — inspect table history and revert changes.

  • API serving — declare HTTP routes alongside tables using FastAPI integration.

Here is an example by Alison Presmanes Hill, PhD builds a photo search application with Pixeltable using six retrieval approaches. It starts with keyword search, then adds LLM query rewriting, hybrid search with BLIP captions and CLIP embeddings, automatic captioning and indexing of new images, metadata filtering, and comparison of two embedding models. The walkthrough also covers query decomposition and serving the application over HTTP. It demonstrates how the retrieval strategy can evolve while Pixeltable manages the underlying data and indexes.



More details are available in the project documentation.

License: Apache-2.0


New Learning Resources

Here are some new learning resources that I came across this week.

Tuning LLM with RL

This video from Prompt Engineering tests whether reinforcement learning can move Qwen3.5-4B closer to Qwen3.5-27B on held-out tasks. It covers LoRA training, GRPO, strict checkers for reward hacking, task selection, and combining model distillation with reinforcement learning.



DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 Explained in 15 Minutes

The following video by Bruno Vega examines DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, including its effort-conditioned output-length penalty, benchmark caveats, token costs, and local inference implications. It also discusses DeepSeek Harness and the Search & Fetch API.



Great Terminal Setup

This walkthrough from DevOps Toolbox presents the free and open-source tools that make up the creator’s terminal workflow. It covers the terminal and multiplexer, Workmux, shell configuration, coding agents, navigation, command history, prompts, the IDE, file exploration, and development environment setup.




Book of the Week

This week’s focus is on a new book — Data Engineering for Multimodal AI by Vasundra Srinivasan. The book explores the infrastructure behind multimodal AI, from data architecture and ingestion to retrieval and production operations. It treats assembling useful context from different data types as a data engineering problem. Each chapter includes a practical playbook that readers can extend, connecting the concepts to an implementation. The focus is on building and operating the pipelines that supply multimodal models with reliable data, with examples spanning cloud-native and on-premises environments.

Topics Covered

  • Data architecture — semantic layers, data contracts, and multimodal storage patterns.

  • Ingestion and transformation — validation and processing across data modalities.

  • Feature engineering — feature extraction, fusion, and multimodal feature stores.

  • Storage and retrieval — vector search, knowledge graphs, and hybrid retrieval.

  • Streaming pipelines — event alignment, adaptive processing, and edge computing.

  • MLOps — versioning, testing, monitoring, and automated retraining.

  • Scaling and serving — distributed processing, inference deployment, and cost management.

  • Governance and security — lineage, privacy, and responsible AI practices.


This book is ideal for data engineers, ML engineers, and MLOps practitioners who want to build and maintain data infrastructure for multimodal AI applications.

The book is available on O’Reilly and Amazon.


Have any questions? Please comment below!

See you next Saturday!

Thanks,

Rami

issues.title: Glyf, Applied AI Tutorials, Financial AI…
issues.html:
Glyf, Applied AI Tutorials, Financial AI in Practice | Issue 110

A weekly curated update on data science and engineering topics and resources.





Rami Krispin
Oct 17, 2026

This week’s agenda:

  • Open Source of the Week - Glyf

  • New learning resources - system design, local inference, TabFM, decision models, n8n automation

  • Book of the week - Financial AI in Practice: A playbook for credit, fraud, and investment systems by Taehun Kim

The newsletter is also available on LinkedIn and Substack.



Open Source of the Week

This week’s focus is on the Glyf project.

Glyf is a new open source project from Kannan Kalidasan that adds a code-first visualization build step to a dbt project. Rather than defining charts in a browser-based BI interface, Glyf keeps chart definitions in SQL and dashboards in YAML alongside the data models that power them. It reads dbt artifacts, resolves model references, validates chart SQL, executes it against the warehouse, and renders charts with Altair. The build produces a static site and chart artifacts that can be reviewed, versioned, and published through an existing delivery workflow. The goal is to make visualizations a declared part of the data pipeline rather than a separate downstream asset.

Project repo: https://github.com/glyf-data/glyf

Key Features

  • dbt-aware chart definitions — resolves ref() and source() references from the dbt manifest before rendering.

  • GGSQL visualizations — combines SQL queries with chart instructions to define visualizations in source files.

  • YAML dashboards and Python macros — composes charts, layout, labels, thresholds, and reusable components as reviewable project files.

  • Build-time validation — checks dbt artifacts, chart files, and SQL execution before a complete build.

  • Static publishing artifacts — produces rendered PNG and SVG charts plus a self-contained static site for deployment.

  • Warehouse support — runs through the dbt profile with DuckDB, Trino, Snowflake, and BigQuery listed as supported adapters.

  • Data-exposure controls — includes row-data modes, PII deny or redact rules, value scanning, per-audience builds, and build provenance.



More details are available in the project documentation.

License: Apache 2.0


New Learning Resources

Here are some new learning resources that I came across this week.

Design Software Systems Like a Senior Engineer – Complete Course

This complete course from freeCodeCamp.org focuses on designing software systems from a senior engineer’s perspective.



Qwen 3.8 27B Just Hit 200 Tokens/s on Mac M5

This video from Cloud Codes examines Lithos AI’s lithos-metal inference engine and its Qwen 3.8-27B benchmark on an M5 Max Mac. It contrasts Metal megakernels and speculative decoding with standard decoding, and distinguishes measured from projected token-per-second results.



Google’s GPT-3 Moment for Databases & Spreadsheets (TabFM)

The following video from Prompt Engineering introduces Google’s TabFM, a zero-shot foundation model for tabular classification and regression. It covers TabFM-Auto, a customer-churn workflow, and how data leakage can produce misleading predictions.



Ollama Decision Models: The End of Jev?!

This video by NeuralNine looks at using Ollama to run local decision models that return structured classifications, selections, or scores. It compares that approach with the hosted Jev product and considers tradeoffs around routing tasks, cost, privacy, and access to inference.



n8n Full Course – Architect Scalable AI Automations from Scratch

This full course from freeCodeCamp.org, taught by Rahul Joshi, builds n8n automation workflows ranging from personalized emails and CRM chatbots to document extraction and lead qualification. It covers AI agents, persistent memory, human approval, error handling, and operations monitoring.




Book of the Week

This week’s focus is on a new book — Financial AI in Practice: A playbook for credit, fraud, and investment systems by Taehun Kim. The book follows financial AI projects from data preparation and modeling through deployment, monitoring, and business decisions. Its four-layer framework connects data assets, modeling, strategy and monitoring, and application delivery. The examples span credit scoring, fraud detection, investment analysis, and customer personalization, with explainability and regulatory constraints considered throughout. The goal is to help readers understand how models fit into the wider systems that use their predictions.

Topics Covered

  • Financial AI architecture — connecting data, models, decision rules, and application workflows

  • Credit scoring — preparing data, engineering features, and deploying an XGBoost pipeline

  • Model monitoring and explainability — tracking changes in data and explaining credit decisions

  • Fraud detection — combining supervised classifiers with autoencoders for anomaly detection

  • Graph analytics — using graph neural networks to identify patterns in transaction networks

  • Investment analysis — pairing quantitative models with LLM-based news analysis

  • Retrieval-augmented generation — grounding portfolio analysis in selected sources and recording decisions

  • Personalization and agents — building customer segments and retention workflows with human approval

  • Business strategy and governance — evaluating ROI, model risk, and operational tradeoffs


This book is ideal for data scientists, ML engineers, financial analysts, and technical leaders who want to build financial AI applications and understand the operational decisions surrounding them.

The book is available on the publisher's website and Amazon.
